personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Colin is defined by an overwhelming, almost compulsive enthusiasm and star-struck adoration of Harry. His voice is breathless, rapid-fire, and filled with questions and exclamations. He is persistent to the point of obliviousness — following Harry to Quidditch practice, memorising his schedule, attempting to photograph him at every opportunity including when Harry is injured on the pitch (Ron vomiting slugs, Harry's rubber arm). He is also defined by a naive courage: he pipes up against Malfoy ('You're just jealous') despite being physically tiny, and he cheerfully deflects Harry's attempts to shake him off. His Muggle-born background and wonder at the wizarding world are explicit and recurring ('It's amazing here, isn't it? I never knew all the odd stuff I could do was magic'). His speech is characteristically short, high-energy, overlapping questions and eager declarations. He also appears in later books (GoF, OotP, HBP) as a loyal DA member, a proud older brother to Dennis, and ultimately a young man who sneaks back underage to fight and dies at the Battle of Hogwarts — showing that his devotion to Harry and Hogwarts was not mere fandom but deeply held loyalty.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In Chamber of Secrets, the film captures the core of Colin's personality well: he appears with his camera, introduces himself breathlessly, explains about his Muggle father, asks Harry for a photo, and snaps pictures at inappropriate moments (Ron vomiting slugs: 'Wow! Can you hold him still, Harry?!'). He is ejected from the hospital wing after enthusing about Harry's Quidditch performance ('That was brilliant today, Harry! Brilliant!'). His eagerness, his camera obsession, and his social obliviousness are all present. In the later films (GoF, OotP, HBP), Colin appears only in crowd scenes and brief mentions — he and Dennis try to bewitch Support Cedric badges, the Creevey brothers are referenced as wanting a match analysis — but has no meaningful dialogue or individual characterisation. His death at the Battle of Hogwarts is rendered wordlessly: Harry sees him being carried by Neville and Oliver Wood. The film does not name him in that scene and does not give the moment any weight beyond a brief visual.
personality_voice.difference: The film captures the surface personality in CoS faithfully — the breathlessness, camera, Muggle-born wonder, and oblivious enthusiasm are all present. However, the extended 'Harry meets Colin' scene is cut (per the non-theatrical exclusion), reducing the first meeting to a shorter version. More significantly, in books 3–7 Colin's personality develops: he becomes a loyal, active DA member who has genuinely internalised his devotion; he is proud of Dennis; he is brave enough to sneak back to fight. None of this personality texture is conveyed in the films beyond brief crowd appearances. The death scene in the film loses all the personality resonance — no name is spoken aloud in the scene, no recognition of his courage in returning underage.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core CoS personality is well-preserved in what the film shows. The penalty is for the erasure of Colin's developed personality across books 3–7: his growth from wide-eyed fan to committed, courageous young man is entirely absent from the films. The DA scenes showing him mastering the Impediment Jinx after effort, his role as an older brother proud of Dennis, and his underage return to fight are all stripped away. What remains is only the 'fan-boy' surface of his year-2 self, which is correct but incomplete as a characterisation across the full series.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for CoS film scenes. Reasonably inferred for later-book personality development based on repeated DA mentions, Dennis scenes, and the Battle of Hogwarts.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Colin serves several distinct narrative functions across the books. In CoS: (1) he is the first victim of the Basilisk, his Petrification marking a turning-point in the threat's escalation; (2) his camera inadvertently saves his life and becomes the clue that helps Harry deduce the monster is a Basilisk ('Colin saw it through his camera'); (3) he is used by Malfoy and Ernie Macmillan as evidence that Harry is dangerous ('That first year, Creevey, was annoying Potter... next thing we know, Creevey's been attacked'), which deepens Harry's social isolation; (4) he functions as comic irritant/foil who simultaneously humanises Harry and embarrasses him. In GoF he escorts Harry from Potions to the champions' photo session — a small but active plot function. In OotP he is a named, active DA member who achieves the Impediment Jinx. In DH he is a named fallen hero whose death is witnessed by Harry.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In CoS the film preserves the key plot functions: Colin is Petrified (his camera is shown and opened by Dumbledore), and Harry explicitly names him in the Basilisk deduction scene ('Colin saw it through his camera'). His role as comic irritant is present. In the final celebration scene he is shown snapping photos, which provides a small visual continuity. In GoF, his scene escorting Harry from Potions is cut entirely. His DA participation is reduced to a background presence — he and Dennis are shown 'exchanging awestruck looks' at the DA meeting and trying to bewitch Cedric badges, but no individual agency. His death in the film is handled as a silent visual — Neville carries the body, Oliver Wood takes it over his shoulder — and his name is never spoken aloud in the scene.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The CoS plot functions are largely preserved. The GoF escort scene is absent (his agency in confronting Snape and standing his ground — 'Please, sir — he's got to take his things with him' — is lost). His DA agency as an active member who works hard and succeeds is reduced to background appearances. His death, which in the books is a named, specific loss that Harry registers and that underscores the cost of the battle, is unnamed and visually brief in the film.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The core CoS narrative role is maintained — he is Petrified, his camera provides the clue, and his role as social embarrassment to Harry is present. However, the GoF escort scene (an active, agentive moment where Colin persists against Snape) is absent, and his OotP DA role is functionally nil in the films. His death loses its narrative weight as a named, specific cost. These are meaningful reductions in agency across the series.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for CoS. Directly evidenced for the absence of GoF escort scene and named death moment.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Colin's primary motivation in the books is straightforward and consistently rendered: he is a Muggle-born boy overwhelmed by the wonder of the magical world, and Harry Potter is the emblem of that world's most extraordinary possibilities. His fandom is not shallow — it is rooted in genuine awe, gratitude (he was thought 'mental' by his family until Hogwarts), and a desire to share this world with his Muggle father via photographs. By later books this motivation deepens: his loyalty to Harry and to Hogwarts becomes something he is willing to act on at personal risk (DA membership, returning underage to the Battle). There is no major internal conflict — he is not a conflicted character — but the shift from fan to genuine ally is a motivational evolution.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film presents his core motivation clearly in CoS: the Muggle-born wonder, the father-and-photographs explanation, and the desire to prove he has met Harry. These are stated explicitly in his dialogue. The deepening of motivation across later books — from fan to loyal fighter — is not present in the films because his character is not given space to develop past his CoS presentation.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The CoS motivation is faithfully rendered. The motivational evolution (fan → committed ally → willing to die for Hogwarts) is entirely absent because the films do not give him the scenes to convey it.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The initial motivation is correct and clearly shown. The absence of the developed motivation is a simplification rather than a distortion — it is 'poorly explained but still the same' in spirit — so the penalty is limited. However, the later motivational depth (willingness to fight and die) is not merely underexplained; it is absent, which counts as a flattening of the character's motivational journey.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for CoS motivations. Reasonably inferred for the motivational evolution from DA and Battle of Hogwarts material.

character_arc.book_baseline: Colin's arc across the series moves from wide-eyed, slightly absurd first-year fan to a Gryffindor who has internalised genuine courage and loyalty. Key arc points: Year 2 — enthusiastic fan, Petrified, recovers; Year 3 — still a devoted fan, now an older figure welcoming his brother Dennis; Year 4 — proud older brother, active participant in Hogwarts events, shows initiative (DA involvement implied by later years); Year 5 — active DA member, works hard to master spells, part of the organised resistance to Umbridge; Years 6-7 — continues as a loyal Hogwarts defender; Battle of Hogwarts — sneaks back underage to fight, is killed. The arc ends in sacrifice.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film shows only the Year 2 starting point of the arc. His recovery from Petrification is shown (he snaps photos at the end-of-year feast). His appearance in GoF with Dennis is reduced to background. His OotP DA work is background. His death in DH is present but unnamed and uncontextualised. The arc's movement — from fan to fighter — is not discernible from the film material.
character_arc.difference: The arc's starting point is present. All subsequent steps are absent or invisible. The ending (sacrifice) is present visually but stripped of its meaning as the conclusion of an arc, since the intervening steps are not shown.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed to the point where only its beginning and its end are present, and the end lacks context. This is an incomplete arc — not the same as a flat arc, since the books clearly show growth. The score reflects that the arc is present in skeleton form but most of its steps are missing.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for starting point and death. Reasonably inferred for the arc's development from book corpus.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Colin's primary relationship is with Harry: it is characterised by one-sided adoration, Harry's exasperated tolerance, and — crucially — a gradual, unspoken shift toward genuine mutual respect and loyalty. Harry's annoyance at Colin in the early books is real, but by OotP he appreciates Colin's dedication in the DA, and by DH he registers Colin's death as a personal loss ('He was tiny in death'). The secondary relationship is with Dennis — Colin is a proud, excitable older brother who transmits his own wonder at Hogwarts to his sibling ('Cool! It was probably the giant squid, Dennis!'). This relationship humanises Colin beyond fandom and shows a tender, nurturing side.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Colin relationship in CoS is faithfully rendered as one-sided adoration met with exasperated tolerance — Harry tells him to get out of the way, snaps at him, but automatically says hello when they pass. Colin's name is mentioned sympathetically in Harry's Basilisk deduction ('Colin saw it through his camera'), which implies some degree of care. The Dennis relationship exists briefly in GoF — Colin calls out to Dennis at the Sorting, they exchange looks — but the warmth and sibling dynamic are not developed. There is no scene equivalent to the books' 'Cool! It was probably the giant squid!' moment of joyful fraternal bonding (this moment is not in the film corpus).
key_relationships.difference: The Harry-Colin dynamic is correctly rendered in CoS. The Dennis relationship is present but thin. The later evolution of Harry's attitude toward Colin (from annoyance to genuine loss) is not present in the films because Harry does not react to Colin's death in a named, emotionally registered way.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The core dynamic is present and correct for CoS. The Dennis relationship is present but underdeveloped. The loss of Harry's evolved regard for Colin (his death going unnamed and unregistered by Harry in the film) weakens the relationship's dramatic function. Penalty is moderate — the foundation is correct, but key relational developments are lost.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for CoS Harry-Colin dynamic and GoF Dennis appearance. Reasonably inferred for later evolution.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Colin's complexity is modest but real. He is not merely a joke character: his persistence is rooted in genuine wonder and a desire to share his magical life with his Muggle father; his courage (piping up at Malfoy, sneaking back to the Battle underage) is entirely genuine and consistent with his character. The books show him mastering DA spells through effort ('after three meetings' hard effort'), which reveals determination beneath the superficial enthusiasm. His death — described in detail, his tiny body carried by Neville and Wood — is given weight as one of the named dead, a reminder that even the minor characters who lived in Harry's peripheral vision had their own full lives and loyalties. The sibling dynamic with Dennis adds emotional texture.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film captures the surface of Colin's complexity in CoS: his obliviousness, his courage in the Malfoy exchange (absent from the theatrical cut per the non-theatrical exclusion note — the courtyard scene with Malfoy and Colin's 'You're just jealous' line does not appear in the film corpus as a confirmed theatrical scene), his Muggle-born backstory. However, the sustained texture that makes Colin more than a joke — his DA effort, his fraternal warmth, his underage return to fight, his named death — is largely absent. What the film retains is recognisable but thin.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film preserves the broadest strokes of Colin's characterisation. The material that elevates him beyond 'eager fan' — his DA dedication, his fraternal relationship with Dennis, his courageous death — is either absent or decontextualised. His death in the film is anonymous (his name is not spoken in the scene), removing the specific emotional weight the books assign to it.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is a significant loss of nuance. The film's Colin is recognisable but one-dimensional: he exists as 'the kid with the camera who hero-worships Harry.' The books' Colin is that, but also a determined DA member, a loving older brother, and a young man who chooses to die for what he believes in. The absence of this material changes how the audience understands the character — he appears to be comic relief whose only function is to embarrass Harry, rather than someone whose fandom was the seed of genuine heroism.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what the film shows and omits. Directly evidenced for the unnamed death scene.

score_caps_applied: Cap 4 (score above 70 not applicable if films preserve only broad identity but remove most defining book characterisation): Applied — total held to 69. The film preserves Colin's broad identity (Muggle-born fan with a camera) but removes the material that defines his fuller characterisation: DA dedication, fraternal warmth, courageous arc, named death.
comparative.key_observations: The film's portrayal of Colin Creevey is faithful at the surface level within Chamber of Secrets — his core traits, voice, motivation, and narrative role in that film are well-rendered. However, across the full series, Colin exists in the films only as a recurring background presence who never develops beyond his year-2 characterisation. The books chart a clear arc from eager fan to determined ally to fallen hero, with meaningful supporting material in his DA work, his relationship with Dennis, and the specific emotional weight of his named death. The films compress all of this into background appearances and an anonymous death scene. The result is a character who is recognisable but fundamentally incomplete — his surface is present, his substance is not.
